metadata.title: Bacterial Community Reconstruction Using A Single Sequencing Reaction

extraction_notes.note: There are no theorem or proof environments; the paper's own results are simulation and wet-lab findings read off figures. Each finding the text states is a claim with rigor numerical; figure captions are not nodes.

The l1 relaxation (2.6) appears inside the sentence citing the basis-pursuit recovery result, so that sentence is an external theorem with the equation nested, not a problem node; (2.7), which the paper solves, is a problem. ClP2 could be a definition of the constraint system; kept a claim since it is derived ('can therefore be expressed').

BCS is never given as one procedure: the introduction states its input/output (AP1, no steps: a single-sentence specification) and Section 2.2 its solver (GPSR on (2.7)); preprocessing (AP3-AP6) is in the appendix. They are linked by uses edges into AP1.
RIP is expanded as 'Robust Isometry Property'; the standard name (Candes-Tao) is Restricted Isometry Property.
S is N x k with S_ij the j-th nucleotide of species i, but A is called k x N with A_ij = 1 iff S_ij = 'A'; for Av = a to make sense the entry should be A_ji (indices transposed).

(B.2) uses j both as free index and as summation index and lacks parentheses; as written d_ij sums to 1 over a read, so its mean is 1/(k-1), not 1 as the text says the normalization ensures (a factor k-1 seems missing).
Symbols are overloaded: P is both the PSSM (2.1) and the peak-position table P(alpha); a_ij and c denote peak height and Gaussian width in Appendix B while a_j, c_j are PSSM entries.

Text says power-law vs uniform are the 'blue and green lines' of Fig. 4B but the caption makes the uniform 16S curve black (green is random sequences); the usable region is bins 125-700 in the text but 100-700 in the Fig. 7 caption; RMSE is defined as the plain l2 norm (no mean); the Fig. 4C caption calls precision the 'fraction of incorrect sequences identified'.

Database curation (2.3), the wet-lab protocol (2.4.1), the prose overview of preprocessing (2.4.2, detailed in the appendix) and the introduction's survey of prior methods carry no stated mathematics and give no nodes.

nodes.name: Compressed sensing problem (underdetermined linear system)
nodes.statement: The classical problem in {\bf CS } is solving an under-determined linear system of equations \begin{equation} \mathcal{A} \textbf{v} = \textbf{b} \end{equation} where $\textbf{v}=(v_1,...,v_N)$ is the vector of unknown variables, $\mathcal{A}$ is the {\it sensing} matrix, often called also the {\it mixing} matrix and $\textbf{b}=(b_1,...,b_k)$ are the measured values of the $k$ equations. The number of variables $N$, is far greater than the number of equations $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Classical CS: solve $\mathcal{A}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}$ with $N$ unknowns far exceeding the $k$ equations.

nodes.name: Classical CS linear system $\mathcal{A}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}$
nodes.statement: \mathcal{A} \textbf{v} = \textbf{b}
nodes.label: eq:cs_classic

nodes.name: Sparsity assumption in compressed sensing
nodes.statement: Here one uses an additional sparsity assumption on the solution - by assuming that we are interested only in solution vectors $\textbf{v}$ with only at most $s$ non-zero entries, for some $s \ll N$.
nodes.statement_short: CS assumes the solution has at most $s\ll N$ non-zero entries.

nodes.name: Compressed sensing recovery with O(s log(N/s)) measurements
nodes.statement: According to the {\bf CS } theory, when the matrix $\mathcal{A}$ satisfy certain conditions, most notably the RIP condition \cite{candes2005stable,candes2005decoding}, one can find the sparsest solution uniquely by using only a logarithmic number of equations, $k = O(s \log(N/s))$, instead of a linear number (N) needed for general solution of a linear system.
nodes.origin_citation: Candes, Romberg & Tao 2006; Donoho 2006; Candes & Tao 2005
assumptions: the matrix $\mathcal{A}$ satisfy certain conditions, most notably the RIP condition \cite{candes2005stable,candes2005decoding}
conclusions: one can find the sparsest solution uniquely by using only a logarithmic number of equations, $k = O(s \log(N/s))$
also_stated_at: Furthermore, it is known that with very high probability a unique and accurate reconstruction is achievable with as few as $O(s \log (N/s))$ measurements, compared to $O(N)$ measurements required for finding a solution for a general linear system without a sparsity assumption \cite{Candes:01,Donoho:01}.
nodes.statement_short: Under RIP, the sparsest solution is recovered uniquely from $k=O(s\log(N/s))$ equations instead of $N$.

nodes.name: Bacterial Compressed Sensing algorithm (BCS)
nodes.statement: The proposed Bacterial Compressed Sensing algorithm ({\textbf {BCS} }\!\!) uses as inputs a database of known 16S rRNA sequences and the measured Sanger-sequence of the unknown mixture, and returns the sparse set of bacteria present in the mixture and their predicted frequencies.
input: a database of known 16S rRNA sequences
the measured Sanger-sequence of the unknown mixture
output: the sparse set of bacteria present in the mixture and their predicted frequencies
nodes.statement_short: BCS: from a 16S rRNA database and one mixed Sanger chromatogram, return the sparse set of species and their frequencies.

nodes.name: Bacterial Community Reconstruction Problem
nodes.statement: In the Bacterial Community Reconstruction Problem we are given a bacterial mixture of unknown composition. In addition, we have at hand a database of the orthologous genomic sequences for a specific known gene, which is assumed to be present in a large number of bacterial species (in our case, the gene used was the 16S rRNA gene). Our purpose is to reconstruct the identity of species present in the mixture, as well as their frequencies, where the assumption is that the sequences for the gene in all or the vast majority of species present in the mixture are available in the database.
nodes.statement_short: Given a mixture of unknown composition and a database of one gene's sequences, recover which species are present and their frequencies.

nodes.name: Linearity of the mixed Sanger chromatogram
nodes.statement: Since Sanger sequencing proceeds independently for each DNA strand present in the sample, the sequence chromatogram of the mixture corresponds to the linear combination of the constituent sequences, where the linear coefficients are proportional to the abundance of each species in the mixture.
nodes.statement_short: The mixture chromatogram is a linear combination of the constituent sequences, weighted by abundance.

nodes.name: Number of database species $N$
nodes.statement: Let $N$ be the number of known bacterial species present in our database.

nodes.name: Species frequency vector $\mathbf{v}$
nodes.statement: Each bacterial population is characterized by a vector ${\textbf v}=(v_1,...,v_N)$ of frequencies of the different species.
differentia: of frequencies of the different species

nodes.name: Number of species present $s$ and the $\ell_0$ norm
nodes.statement: Denote by $s$ the number of species present in the sample $s=\|{\textbf v}\|_{\ell 0}$, where $\|.\|_{\ell 0}$ denotes the $\ell_0$ norm which simply counts the number of non-zero elements of a vector $\|{\textbf v}\|_{\ell 0} = \sum_i 1_{\{v_i \neq 0\}}$.
nodes.statement_short: $s=\|\mathbf{v}\|_{\ell 0}$, the number of non-zero entries of $\mathbf{v}$.

nodes.name: Sparsity of bacterial communities
nodes.statement: While the total number of known species $N$ is usually very large (in our case on the order of tens to hundreds of thousands), a typical bacterial community consists of a small subset of the species, and therefore in a given sample, $s \ll N$, and ${\textbf v}$ is a sparse vector.
also_stated_at: The sparseness assumption in our scenario is obtained by noting that although numerous species of bacteria have been characterized and are present on earth, at a given sample typically only a small fraction of them are present at significant levels, while the proportion of all other species is essentially zero.

The crucial assumption we make in order to cope with the insufficiency of information is the sparsity of the vector $\textbf{v}$, which reflects the fact that only a small number of species are present in the mixture.
nodes.statement_short: A community contains a small subset of the $N$ known species, so $s\ll N$ and $\mathbf{v}$ is sparse.

nodes.name: Database sequence matrix $S$
nodes.statement: The database sequences are denoted by a matrix $S$, where $S_{ij}$ is the $j$'th nucleotide in the orthologous sequence of the $i$'th species ($i=1,..,N, j=1,..,k$).

nodes.name: Position-specific score matrix (PSSM) of the mixture
nodes.statement: We represent the results of the mixture Sanger sequencing of length $k$ as a $4 \times k$ Position-specific-Score-Matrix (PSSM) \begin{equation} P = \begin{pmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & \cdots & a_k \\ c_1 & c_2 & \cdots & c_k \\ g_1 & g_2 & \cdots & g_k \\ t_1 & t_2 & \cdots & t_k \\ \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} {\textbf a} \\ {\textbf c} \\ {\textbf g} \\ {\textbf t} \\ \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} where ${\textbf p}_j=(a_j, c_j, g_j, t_j)^t$ is a column vector representing the observed frequencies at sequence position $j$ of the four nucleotides, with $a_j,c_j,g_j,t_j \geq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: The mixed Sanger read of length $k$ is a $4\times k$ PSSM whose column $j$ holds the observed nucleotide frequencies $(a_j,c_j,g_j,t_j)$.

nodes.name: PSSM $P$ with rows $\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{g},\mathbf{t}$
nodes.statement: P = \begin{pmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & \cdots & a_k \\ c_1 & c_2 & \cdots & c_k \\ g_1 & g_2 & \cdots & g_k \\ t_1 & t_2 & \cdots & t_k \\ \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} {\textbf a} \\ {\textbf c} \\ {\textbf g} \\ {\textbf t} \\ \end{pmatrix}
nodes.label: eq:PSSM

nodes.name: A zero-frequency position excludes species
nodes.statement: For example, if at a certain position $j$, the frequency $a_j$ of '$A$' in the mixed sequence is $0$, and assuming no measurement noise is present, it follows that all bacteria which have '$A$' at the $j$'th position of their orthologous gene are not present in the mixture.
nodes.statement_short: If $a_j=0$ (no noise), every species with A at position $j$ is absent.

nodes.name: Per-position linear constraint on the mixture
nodes.statement: More generally, the frequency of each nucleotide at a given position $j$ gives a linear constraint on the mixture: \begin{equation} \sum_{i=1}^N v_i 1_{\{ S_{ij} = '\!A' \}} = a_j \end{equation} and similarly for $'\!C','\!G','\!T'$.
conclusions: the frequency of each nucleotide at a given position $j$ gives a linear constraint on the mixture
nodes.statement_short: Each nucleotide frequency at position $j$ equals the total frequency of species carrying that nucleotide there.

nodes.name: Mixture matrices $A, C, G, T$
nodes.statement: Define the $k \times N$ mixture matrix $A$ for the nucleotide '${A}$': \begin{equation} A_{ij}=\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1 & S_{ij} = '\!\!{A}' \\ 0 & \mbox{otherwise} \end{array} \right. \end{equation} and similarly for the nucleotides $'\!{C}','\!{G}','\!{T}'$.
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is the binary $k\times N$ indicator of nucleotide A in the database sequences; likewise $C,G,T$.

nodes.name: Mixture matrix entries $A_{ij}$
nodes.statement: A_{ij}=\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1 & S_{ij} = '\!\!{A}' \\ 0 & \mbox{otherwise} \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: eq:MixMatrix

nodes.name: Sequencing constraints as a linear system
nodes.statement: The constraints given by the sequencing reaction can therefore be expressed as: \begin{equation} A\textbf{v}=\textbf{a}, C\textbf{v}=\textbf{c}, G\textbf{v}=\textbf{g}, T\textbf{v}=\textbf{t} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The sequencing data give the four linear systems $A\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{a}$, ..., $T\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{t}$.

nodes.name: BCS linear constraints $A\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{a},\dots,T\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{t}$
nodes.statement: A\textbf{v}=\textbf{a}, C\textbf{v}=\textbf{c}, G\textbf{v}=\textbf{g}, T\textbf{v}=\textbf{t}
nodes.label: eq:LinConstraints

nodes.name: The reconstruction system is underdetermined
nodes.statement: Hence, from a single sequencing reaction of length $k$ we derive a set of $4k$ linear equations. Since a typical sequencing reaction is of length $k \sim 500\!-\! 1000$, the total number of equations is $4k \sim 2000 \! - \! 4000$. This is still considerably smaller than the number of free variables $N$ which is on the order of tens to hundreds of thousands. Hence, this is an underdetermined linear system, and without further assumptions we are not guaranteed a single solution.
nodes.statement_short: A read gives $4k\sim 2000$-$4000$ equations, far fewer than $N$, so the system is underdetermined.

nodes.name: $\ell_0$ sparse reconstruction problem
nodes.statement: We seek a sparse solution for the set of equations (\ref{eq:LinConstraints}). Such a solution provides a small set of species which is consistent with the measured data. In the {\bf CS } paradigm, one can formulate the quest for the sparsest solution satisfying the given set of linear constraints as follows: \begin{equation} \textbf{v}^*= \underset{\textbf{v}}{argmin}\|\textbf{v}\|_{\ell 0} \quad s.t. \quad A\textbf{v}=\textbf{a}, C\textbf{v}=\textbf{c}, G\textbf{v}=\textbf{g}, T\textbf{v}=\textbf{t} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Find the sparsest $\mathbf{v}$ satisfying the four nucleotide constraint systems.

nodes.name: $\ell_0$ minimization (2.5)
nodes.statement: \textbf{v}^*= \underset{\textbf{v}}{argmin}\|\textbf{v}\|_{\ell 0} \quad s.t. \quad A\textbf{v}=\textbf{a}, C\textbf{v}=\textbf{c}, G\textbf{v}=\textbf{g}, T\textbf{v}=\textbf{t}
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
nodes.label: eq:L0Min

nodes.name: BCS reduces to the classical CS problem
nodes.statement: The formulation above can be easily seen as a {\bf CS } problem - one can in principle construct a big 'sensing' matrix $\mathcal{A}_{4k\times N}$ as a simple concatenation of the matrices A,C,G,T, and similarly a measurements vector $\textbf{b}$ as a concatenation of the measurements $\textbf{a}, \textbf{c}, \textbf{g}$ and $\textbf{t}$, and with these notations problem (\ref{eq:L0Min}) is in fact reduced to the classic {\bf CS } problem \cite{Candes:01} of finding the sparsest solution for eq. (\ref{eq:cs_classic}).
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
assumptions: one can in principle construct a big 'sensing' matrix $\mathcal{A}_{4k\times N}$ as a simple concatenation of the matrices A,C,G,T, and similarly a measurements vector $\textbf{b}$ as a concatenation of the measurements $\textbf{a}, \textbf{c}, \textbf{g}$ and $\textbf{t}$
conclusions: problem (\ref{eq:L0Min}) is in fact reduced to the classic {\bf CS } problem \cite{Candes:01} of finding the sparsest solution for eq. (\ref{eq:cs_classic})
nodes.statement_short: Stacking $A,C,G,T$ into a $4k\times N$ sensing matrix turns (2.5) into the classical sparsest-solution CS problem.

nodes.name: NP-hardness of $\ell_0$ minimization
nodes.statement: From a practical point of view, problem (\ref{eq:L0Min}) is known to be in general NP-Hard \cite{candes2005error}, and hence finding the optimal solution is not computationally feasible.
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
conclusions: problem (\ref{eq:L0Min}) is known to be in general NP-Hard \cite{candes2005error}
nodes.statement_short: Exact $\ell_0$ minimization is NP-hard in general.

nodes.name: $\ell_1$ convex relaxation recovers the sparse solution (basis pursuit)
nodes.statement: However, a remarkable breakthrough of the {\bf CS } theory shows that under certain conditions on the mixture matrix and the number of measurements (see below), the sparse solution can be recovered uniquely by solving a convex relaxation of the problem, which is obtained by replacing the $\ell 0$ norm with the ''closest'' convex $\ell p$ norm, namely the $\ell 1$ norm, leading to the following minimization problem \cite{candes2006near,donoho2006most,tropp_just_2006}: \begin{equation} \textbf{v}^*=\underset{\textbf{v}}{argmin}\|\textbf{v}\|_{\ell 1} = \underset{\textbf{v}}{argmin}\sum_{i=1}^N |v_i| \quad s.t. \quad A\textbf{v}=\textbf{a}, C\textbf{v}=\textbf{c}, G\textbf{v}=\textbf{g}, T\textbf{v}=\textbf{t} \end{equation} which is a convex optimization problem whose solution can be obtained in polynomial time.
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
assumptions: under certain conditions on the mixture matrix and the number of measurements (see below)
conclusions: the sparse solution can be recovered uniquely by solving a convex relaxation of the problem, which is obtained by replacing the $\ell 0$ norm with the ''closest'' convex $\ell p$ norm, namely the $\ell 1$ norm
which is a convex optimization problem whose solution can be obtained in polynomial time
nodes.statement_short: Under suitable conditions the sparse solution is recovered uniquely by the polynomial-time $\ell_1$ minimization (2.6).

nodes.name: $\ell_1$ minimization (2.6)
nodes.statement: \textbf{v}^*=\underset{\textbf{v}}{argmin}\|\textbf{v}\|_{\ell 1} = \underset{\textbf{v}}{argmin}\sum_{i=1}^N |v_i| \quad s.t. \quad A\textbf{v}=\textbf{a}, C\textbf{v}=\textbf{c}, G\textbf{v}=\textbf{g}, T\textbf{v}=\textbf{t}
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
nodes.label: eq:L1Min

nodes.name: Robustness of compressed sensing to measurement noise
nodes.statement: Fortunately, the {\bf CS } paradigm is known to be robust to measurement noise \cite{candes2005stable,candes2007dantzig}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
nodes.origin_citation: Candes, Romberg & Tao 2006 (stable recovery); Candes & Tao 2007 (Dantzig selector)
conclusions: the {\bf CS } paradigm is known to be robust to measurement noise

nodes.name: Noise-tolerant BCS problem ($\ell_2$ fit plus $\ell_1$ penalty)
nodes.statement: One can cope with noise by enabling a trade-off between sparseness and accuracy in the reconstruction merit function, which in our case is formulated as: \begin{equation} \textbf{v}^* = \underset{\textbf{v}}{argmin} \:\: \frac{1}{2} \big( \|{\textbf a}-A\textbf{v}\|^2_{\ell 2} + \|{\textbf c}-C\textbf{v}\|^2_{\ell 2} + \|{\textbf g}-G\textbf{v}\|^2_{\ell 2} + \|{\textbf t}-T\textbf{v}\|^2_{\ell 2} \big) + \tau \|\textbf{v}\|_{\ell 1} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Minimize half the squared $\ell_2$ misfit of the four constraint systems plus $\tau\|\mathbf{v}\|_1$.

nodes.name: $\ell_2$-$\ell_1$ objective (2.7)
nodes.statement: \textbf{v}^* = \underset{\textbf{v}}{argmin} \:\: \frac{1}{2} \big( \|{\textbf a}-A\textbf{v}\|^2_{\ell 2} + \|{\textbf c}-C\textbf{v}\|^2_{\ell 2} + \|{\textbf g}-G\textbf{v}\|^2_{\ell 2} + \|{\textbf t}-T\textbf{v}\|^2_{\ell 2} \big) + \tau \|\textbf{v}\|_{\ell 1}
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
nodes.label: eq:GPSR

nodes.name: Role of $\tau$ and relation of (2.7) to (2.6)
nodes.statement: This problem represents a more general form of eq. (\ref{eq:L1Min}), and accounts for noise in the measurement process. This is utilized by insertion of an $\ell 2$ quadratic error term. Importantly, even with the addition of the $\ell 2$ term the problem (\ref{eq:GPSR}) is still a convex optimization problem. The parameter $\tau$ determines the relative weight of the error term vs. the sparsity promoting term. Increasing $\tau$ leads to a sparser solution, at the price of a worse fit for the measurement equations, whereas decreasing $\tau$ leads to a better fit to the equations, while possibly requiring more non-zero elements in the solution (for low enough values of $\tau$ we can fit the equations in (\ref{eq:L1Min}) precisely, and the $\ell 2$ error term vanishes, thus the problem is reduced back to eq. (\ref{eq:L1Min})).
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
nodes.statement_short: (2.7) generalizes (2.6) and stays convex; larger $\tau$ gives sparser, worse-fitting solutions, and small $\tau$ recovers (2.6).

nodes.name: BCS solver: GPSR on problem (2.7)
nodes.statement: Many algorithms which enable an efficient solution of problem (\ref{eq:GPSR}) are available, and we have chosen the widely used GPSR algorithm described in \cite{GPSR:01}. The error tolerance parameter was set to $\tau=10$ for the simulated mixture reconstruction, and $\tau=100$ for the reconstruction of the experimental mixture.
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Solve (2.7) with the GPSR algorithm, $\tau=10$ for simulated and $\tau=100$ for experimental mixtures.

nodes.name: Call GPSR
nodes.statement: Many algorithms which enable an efficient solution of problem (\ref{eq:GPSR}) are available, and we have chosen the widely used GPSR algorithm described in \cite{GPSR:01}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Solve (2.7) with GPSR.

nodes.name: Set $\tau$
nodes.statement: The error tolerance parameter was set to $\tau=10$ for the simulated mixture reconstruction, and $\tau=100$ for the reconstruction of the experimental mixture.
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
nodes.statement_short: $\tau=10$ (simulation), $\tau=100$ (experiment).

nodes.name: Robustness of BCS to the choice of $\tau$
nodes.statement: These values achieved a rather sparse solution in most cases (a few species reconstructed with frequencies above zero), while still giving a good sensitivity. The performance of the algorithm was quite robust to the specific value of $\tau$ used, and therefore further optimization of the results by fine tuning $\tau$ was not followed in this study.
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
nodes.statement_short: The chosen $\tau$ gives sparse, sensitive solutions and performance is robust to $\tau$.

nodes.name: Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) / Uniform Uncertainty Principle (UUP)
nodes.statement: The most well-known condition for successful reconstruction is the 'Robust Isometry Property' (RIP), also known as the 'Uniform Uncertainty Principle' (UUP) \cite{candes2005stable,candes2005decoding}. Briefly, RIP for a matrix means that any subset of $2s$ columns of the matrix $\mathcal{A}$ is 'almost orthogonal' (although since $k < N$ the columns cannot be perfectly orthogonal). This property makes the matrix $\mathcal{A}$ 'invertible' for sparse vectors $v$ with sparsity $s$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
differentia: any subset of $2s$ columns of the matrix $\mathcal{A}$ is 'almost orthogonal'
nodes.statement_short: RIP: every set of $2s$ columns of the sensing matrix is almost orthogonal, so the matrix is invertible on $s$-sparse vectors.

nodes.name: A few thousand measurements suffice for a few dozen species
nodes.statement: In our case the number of measurements $4k$ is on order of a few thousands, thus these results suggest that accurate reconstruction is possible, at least when the sparsity $s$ in the range of a few dozens.
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
assumptions: the number of measurements $4k$ is on order of a few thousands
conclusions: accurate reconstruction is possible, at least when the sparsity $s$ in the range of a few dozens

nodes.name: The BCS mixing matrix is predetermined and coherent
nodes.statement: One important difference between classical {\bf CS } and our problem is the structure of the mixing matrix $\mathcal{A}$. In our application the mixing matrix represents the sequence database $S$ which is pre-determined. Moreover, for species which are close in the bacterial phylogeny, the gene sequences in the database exhibit high sequence similarity and therefore the corresponding columns in the sensing matrix are far from orthogonal. It is thus far from clear in advance that the given mixing matrix posses the desired properties to enable successful reconstruction. This point is addressed in the Results section.
nodes.section: 2.2 Mapping the Problem to Compressed Sensing - the {\textbf {BCS} } Algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Unlike designed CS matrices, the BCS mixing matrix is fixed by the database and has near-parallel columns for related species.

nodes.name: Simulated mixture reconstruction protocol
nodes.statement: In order to asses the performance of the proposed {\textbf {BCS} } reconstruction algorithm, random subsets of species from the greengene database \cite{desantis2006greengenes} were selected. Within these subsets, the relative frequencies of each species were drawn at random from a uniform frequency distribution (normalized to sum to one), and a mixed sequence PSSM was calculated (results for a different, power-law frequency distribution, are shown later). This PSSM was then used as the input for the {\textbf {BCS} } algorithm, which returned the frequencies of database sequences predicted to participate in the mixture (see Methods section and Figure \ref{fig:MethodScheme}).
output: the frequencies of database sequences predicted to participate in the mixture
nodes.statement_short: Draw random species subsets with uniform random frequencies, compute the mixed PSSM, and reconstruct it with BCS.

nodes.name: Select random species
nodes.statement: In order to asses the performance of the proposed {\textbf {BCS} } reconstruction algorithm, random subsets of species from the greengene database \cite{desantis2006greengenes} were selected.
nodes.statement_short: Pick a random subset of database species.

nodes.name: Draw frequencies and compute PSSM
nodes.statement: Within these subsets, the relative frequencies of each species were drawn at random from a uniform frequency distribution (normalized to sum to one), and a mixed sequence PSSM was calculated (results for a different, power-law frequency distribution, are shown later).
nodes.statement_short: Uniform random frequencies, normalized; compute the mixed PSSM.

nodes.name: Run BCS
nodes.statement: This PSSM was then used as the input for the {\textbf {BCS} } algorithm, which returned the frequencies of database sequences predicted to participate in the mixture (see Methods section and Figure \ref{fig:MethodScheme}).
nodes.statement_short: Reconstruct the frequencies with BCS.

nodes.name: Sample simulated reconstruction of 10 species
nodes.statement: The {\textbf {BCS} } algorithm successfully identified all of the species present in the original mixture, as well as several false positives (species not present in the original mixture). The largest false positive frequency was $0.01$, with a total fraction of $0.04$ false positives.
nodes.statement_short: On a 10-species mixture with 500 bp, BCS finds all species plus small false positives (max 0.01, total 0.04).

nodes.name: Reconstruction RMSE
nodes.statement: RMSE is the Root-Mean Squared-Error between the original mixture vector and the reconstructed vector, defined as $RMSE = \|\textbf{v}-\textbf{v}^*\|_{\ell 2} = \Big(\sum_{i=1}^N (v_i-v^*_i)^2\Big)^{1/2}$.
nodes.genus: Root-Mean Squared-Error between the original mixture vector and the reconstructed vector
nodes.statement_short: RMSE $=\|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{v}^*\|_2$.

nodes.name: Recall and precision of a reconstruction
nodes.statement: As another measure, we have recorded the {\it recall}, defined as the fraction of species present in the original vector $\textbf{v}$ which were also present in the reconstructed vector $\textbf{v}^*$ (this is also known as sensitivity), and the {\it precision}, defined as the fraction of species present in the reconstructed vector $\textbf{v}^*$ which were also present in the original mixture vector $\textbf{v}$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall: fraction of true species recovered; precision: fraction of reconstructed species that are true.

nodes.name: Minimal frequency threshold for calling a species present
nodes.statement: Since the predicted frequency is a continuous variable, whereas the recall/precision relies on a binary categorization, a minimal threshold for calling a species present in the reconstructed mixture was used before calculating the recall/precision scores.
nodes.definiendum: minimal threshold for calling a species present

nodes.name: Insertions and deletions decorrelate orthologous sequences
nodes.statement: In our case this cannot be achieved, as we were given the sequences determining the mixing matrix and cannot control them. Even though the sequences are orthologous and thus quite similar, insertions and deletions came to our aid, as they bring similar sequences to being out of phase (for example, even a deletion of a single base from a sequence, reduces its correlation with a copy of itself from one to a number typically much lower).
nodes.statement_short: The database columns cannot be designed, but indels shift similar sequences out of phase and lower their correlation.

nodes.name: Mutual coherence of a mixing matrix
nodes.statement: It has been previously shown \cite{ben-haim_near-oracle_2009,tropp_just_2006} that a computationally feasible method for assessing the information content of the mixing matrix is the mutual coherence, defined as the maximal coherence (inner product) between two columns of the mixing matrix.
nodes.genus: maximal coherence (inner product) between two columns of the mixing matrix

nodes.name: Coherence distribution of 16S rRNA database columns
nodes.statement: The distribution of coherence values for random pairs of database species is shown in Figure \ref{fig:Coherence}. While most correlations are centered around $0.25$, there exists a small fraction of highly correlated sequences, with $0.005$ of the sequence pairs showing a correlation above $0.8$, and a maximal correlation value of $0.998$.
nodes.statement_short: Pairwise coherences centre at 0.25, but 0.5% of pairs exceed 0.8 and the maximum is 0.998.

nodes.name: High coherence limits worst-case reconstruction only
nodes.statement: This high mutual coherence value places a limit on the reconstruction performance in the worst case, when such a sequence is present in the mixture. Since the database contains another highly similar sequence, distinguishing between these two is very difficult, and therefore the {\bf CS } reconstruction cannot guarantee complete accuracy. However, given that such similar sequences are typically of closely related species (thus not being able to distinguish between them may be considered acceptable), and since most of the sequences show near random coherence, the reconstruction in most of the cases may still require only a small number of measurements (which translates into a small number of nucleotides read in the sequencing).
nodes.statement_short: Near-duplicate sequences cannot be told apart, but they are usually close relatives and most pairs are near-random, so few measurements suffice.

nodes.name: About 300 nucleotides suffice for 10 species
nodes.statement: It is shown in Figure \ref{fig:SeqNum}.A that using longer sequence lengths results in a larger number of linear constraints and therefore higher accuracy, with $\sim\! 300$ nucleotides sufficing for accurate reconstruction of a mixture of 10 sequences.
nodes.statement_short: Longer reads give more constraints and accuracy; about 300 nt reconstruct a 10-species mixture accurately.

nodes.name: Random nucleotide sequence database
nodes.statement: In order to asses the effect of the dependence between the database sequences (which leads to high coherence of the mixing matrix columns) on the performance of the {\textbf {BCS} } algorithm, a similar mixture simulation was performed using a database of random nucleotide sequences (i.e. each sequence was composed of i.i.d. nucleotides with $0.25$ probability for 'A','C','G' or 'T').
differentia: each sequence was composed of i.i.d. nucleotides with $0.25$ probability for 'A','C','G' or 'T'

nodes.name: Coherence of random sequence databases
nodes.statement: Since sequences were independently drawn, the pairwise correlation values are centered around $0.25$, with maximal coherence value less than $0.4$ over all pairs we have simulated (data not shown).

nodes.name: Random sequences need about 100 nucleotides
nodes.statement: Using a mixing matrix derived from these random sequences, the {\textbf {BCS} } reconstruction algorithm showed better performance (green line in Figure \ref{fig:SeqNum}.A), with $\sim\! 100$ nucleotides sufficing for a similar RMSE as that obtained for the 16S rRNA database using $300$ nucleotides.
nodes.statement_short: With an i.i.d. random database, about 100 nt match the RMSE that the 16S database reaches with 300 nt.

nodes.name: Reconstruction of 100-species mixtures
nodes.statement: Even on a mixture of $100$ species, the reconstruction showed an average RMSE less than $0.04$, with the highest false positive reconstructed frequency (i.e. frequency for species not present in the original mixture) being less than $0.01$. Using a minimal frequency threshold of $0.0025$ for calling a species present in the reconstruction, the {\textbf {BCS} } algorithm shows an average recall of $0.75$ and a precision of $0.85$.
nodes.statement_short: At $k=500$, 100-species mixtures give RMSE below 0.04, and recall 0.75 / precision 0.85 at threshold 0.0025.

nodes.name: 16S rRNA sequences suffice for mixtures of tens of species
nodes.statement: Therefore, while the sequence database did not perform as well as random sequences, the 16S rRNA sequences exhibit enough variation to enable a successful reconstruction of mixtures of tens of species with a small percent of errors.
nodes.statement_short: Although worse than random sequences, 16S rRNA varies enough to reconstruct mixtures of tens of species.

nodes.name: Power-law species frequency distribution
nodes.statement: We therefore tested the performance of the {\textbf {BCS} } reconstruction on a similar power-law distribution of species frequencies with with $v_i \sim i^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Power-law mixtures: RMSE similar to uniform
nodes.statement: Performance on such a power-law mixture is similar to the uniformly distibuted mixture (blue and green lines in Figure \ref{fig:SeqNum}.B respectively) in terms of the RMSE.

nodes.name: Power-law mixtures: recall/precision up to 50 species
nodes.statement: The recall/precision of the {\textbf {BCS} } algorithm on such mixtures (Figure \ref{fig:PowerlawReconstruction}.C) is similar to the uniform distribution for mixtures containing up to 50 species, with degrading performance on larger mixtures, due to the long tail of low frequency species.
nodes.statement_short: On power-law mixtures recall/precision match the uniform case up to 50 species and degrade beyond, due to the long tail.

nodes.name: Additive Gaussian measurement-noise model
nodes.statement: Measurement noise was modeled as additive i.i.d. Gaussian noise $z_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ applied to each PSSM element in eq. (\ref{eq:PSSM}).
nodes.statement_short: Each PSSM entry gets i.i.d. $N(0,\sigma^2)$ additive noise.

nodes.name: Reconstruction degrades slowly with noise
nodes.statement: The reconstruction performance slowly degrades with added noise both for the real 16S rRNA and the random sequence database.

nodes.name: Reconstruction at the experimental noise level $\sigma=0.15$
nodes.statement: Using a noise standard deviation of $\sigma=0.15$ (which is the approximate experimental noise level - see later) and sequencing $500$ nucleotides, the reconstruction performance as a function of the number of species in the mixture is shown in Figure \ref{fig:SampReconstruction}. Under this noise level, the {\textbf {BCS} } algorithm reconstructed a mixture of 40 sequences with an average RMSE of $0.07$ (Figure \ref{fig:SampReconstruction}.B), compared to $\sim\!0.02$ when no noise is present (Figure \ref{fig:SeqNum}.B). By using a minimal frequency threshold of $0.006$ for the predicted mixture, {\textbf {BCS} } showed a recall (sensitivity) of $\sim\! 0.7$, with a precision of $\sim\! 0.7$ (see Figure \ref{fig:SampReconstruction}.B), attained under realistic noise levels.
nodes.statement_short: With $\sigma=0.15$ and 500 nt, a 40-species mixture gives RMSE 0.07 and recall and precision about 0.7 at threshold 0.006.

nodes.name: Graceful degradation under realistic noise
nodes.statement: To conclude, we have observed that the addition of noise leads to a graceful degradation in the reconstruction performance, and one can still achieve accurate reconstruction with realistic noise levels.

nodes.name: Local-sequence correction reduces peak prediction error
nodes.statement: The distribution of relative peak height and position errors following local sequence correction is shown in blue bars in Figure \ref{fig:SampleChromatogram}.B,C, and the standard deviation is reduced to $0.15$ and $0.75$ for peak height and position respectively.
nodes.statement_short: 6-mer context correction reduces the SD of peak height and position errors from 0.26 and 1.3 to 0.15 and 0.75.

nodes.name: Predicted mixture chromatogram accuracy on bins 125-700
nodes.statement: On the region of bins 125-700 the prediction shows high accuracy, with an average root square error of 0.08.

nodes.name: Reconstruction of a five-species experimental mixture
nodes.statement: The algorithm successfully identifies three of the five bacteria (\textit{Vibrio fischeri, Enterococcus faecalis} and \textit{Photobacterium leiognathi}). Out of the two remaining strains, one (\textit{Staphylococcus epidermidis}) is identified at the genus level, and the other (\textit{Escherichia coli}) is mistakenly identified as \textit{Salmonella enterica}.
nodes.statement_short: From one Sanger read of a 5-strain mixture BCS finds 3 strains, one more to genus level, and confuses E. coli with S. enterica.

nodes.name: E. coli recovered once its sequence is in the database
nodes.statement: While \textit{Escherichia coli} and \textit{Salmonella enterica} show a sequence difference in 33 bases over the PCR amplified region, only two bases are different in the region used for the {\textbf {BCS} } reconstruction, and thus the \textit{Escherichia coli} sequence was removed in the database preprocessing stage. When this sequence is manually added to the database (in addition to the \textit{Salmonella enterica} sequence), the {\textbf {BCS} } algorithm correctly identifies the presence of \textit{Escherichia coli} rather than \textit{Salmonella enterica} in the mixture.
nodes.statement_short: E. coli was removed as a near-duplicate of S. enterica in the used region; re-adding it lets BCS identify E. coli correctly.

nodes.name: One read suffices even for databases of millions of sequences
nodes.statement: Essentially, the amount of information needed for identifying the species present in the mixture is logarithmic in the database size \cite{Candes:01,Donoho:01}, as long as the number of the species present in the mixture is kept constant. Therefore, a single sequencing reaction with hundreds of bases contains in principle a very large amount of information and should suffice for unique reconstruction even when the database contains millions of different sequences.
assumptions: as long as the number of the species present in the mixture is kept constant
conclusions: the amount of information needed for identifying the species present in the mixture is logarithmic in the database size

a single sequencing reaction with hundreds of bases contains in principle a very large amount of information and should suffice for unique reconstruction even when the database contains millions of different sequences

nodes.name: Non-negativity of frequencies is not enforced
nodes.statement: In the current implementation, the fact that bacteria have only non-negative frequencies was not explicitly enforced in eq. (\ref{eq:GPSR}). Utilizing this information is known to simplify the reconstruction problem \cite{Donoho:positive}, and we expect it to lead to more efficient and accurate reconstruction.
nodes.statement_short: (2.7) does not enforce $\mathbf{v}\ge 0$; adding it is known to simplify recovery and is expected to help.

nodes.name: Extension to several sequencing reactions
nodes.statement: The proposed method can easily be extended to more than one sequencing reaction per mixture, by simply joining all sequencing results as linear constraints. Such extension can lead to a larger number of linear constraints, and thus increasing accuracy in cases such as when deciphering larger mixtures in the presence of experimental noise.

nodes.name: Chromatogram trace vectors $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{c},\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{t}$
nodes.statement: The input to the chromatogram preprocessing is the measured chromatogram, consisting of four fluorescent trace vectors $\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{c},\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{t}$, where for example $\mathfrak{a}_p$ represents the signal intensity for nucleotide $'A'$ at the $p$'s position along the chromatogram, where each position is represented by one pixel in the chromatogram image.
nodes.statement_short: The measured chromatogram is four trace vectors; $\mathfrak{a}_p$ is the A-signal intensity at pixel $p$.

nodes.name: Chromatogram Preprocessing
nodes.statement:
oindent { f Algorithm:} Chromatogram Preprocessing \ 
oindent { f Input:} $(\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{c},\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{t})$ - four fluorescent trace vectors \ 
oindent { f Output:} $P = (a, c, g, t)^t$ - a PSSM representing nucleotide frequencies  egin{enumerate} \item Normalize the chromatogram amplitude:  egin{equation} \mathfrak{a}_p =  rac{50 \cdot 12 \cdot \mathfrak{a}_p}{\sum_{q=-25 \cdot 12}^{25 \cdot 12} (\mathfrak{a}_{p+q} + \mathfrak{c}_{p+q} + \mathfrak{g}_{p+q} + \mathfrak{t}_{p+q})} \end{equation} and similarly for $\mathfrak{c}_p$,$\mathfrak{g}_p$ and $\mathfrak{t}_p$. \item bin into constant sized bins, average bin values and apply square root transformation:  egin{equation} a_i = \sqrt{\sum_{p=12i}^{12i+11}\mathfrak{a}_p} \:, \quad i=1...k \end{equation} and similarly for $c_i$,$g_i$,$t_i$.
output: $P = (a, c, g, t)^t$ - a PSSM representing nucleotide frequencies
nodes.statement_short: Turn a mixed chromatogram into a PSSM: normalize amplitude by a 50 bp running total, then sum 12-pixel bins and take square roots.

nodes.name: Normalize amplitude
nodes.statement: Normalize the chromatogram amplitude: \begin{equation} \mathfrak{a}_p = \frac{50 \cdot 12 \cdot \mathfrak{a}_p}{\sum_{q=-25 \cdot 12}^{25 \cdot 12} (\mathfrak{a}_{p+q} + \mathfrak{c}_{p+q} + \mathfrak{g}_{p+q} + \mathfrak{t}_{p+q})} \end{equation} and similarly for $\mathfrak{c}_p$,$\mathfrak{g}_p$ and $\mathfrak{t}_p$.
nodes.statement_short: Divide each trace by the total intensity in a 50 bp window.

nodes.name: Bin and square-root
nodes.statement: bin into constant sized bins, average bin values and apply square root transformation: \begin{equation} a_i = \sqrt{\sum_{p=12i}^{12i+11}\mathfrak{a}_p} \:, \quad i=1...k \end{equation} and similarly for $c_i$,$g_i$,$t_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Sum 12-pixel bins and take the square root to get PSSM column $i$.

nodes.name: Amplitude normalization (A.1)
nodes.statement: \mathfrak{a}_p = \frac{50 \cdot 12 \cdot \mathfrak{a}_p}{\sum_{q=-25 \cdot 12}^{25 \cdot 12} (\mathfrak{a}_{p+q} + \mathfrak{c}_{p+q} + \mathfrak{g}_{p+q} + \mathfrak{t}_{p+q})}
nodes.label: eq:normalization_seq_position

nodes.name: Square-root binning (A.2)
nodes.statement: a_i = \sqrt{\sum_{p=12i}^{12i+11}\mathfrak{a}_p} \:, \quad i=1...k
nodes.label: eq:sqrt_binning

nodes.name: Database Preprocessing scheme
nodes.statement: The database preprocessing therefore contains two steps: \begin{enumerate} \item A preliminary step: Compute local-sequence adjusted chromatogram statistics. \\ Here we use a training set $S'$ of known sequences and their chromatograms as input and compute tables $H$ and $P$ representing chromatogram peak heights and positions, respectively, for different local-sequence contexts. \item Database PSSMs Generation step: Generate a database of predicted PSSMs. \\ Here the input is a set $S$ of $N$ sequences and the pre-computed tables $H$ and $P$. The sequence input and tables are used to determine peak heights and positions and compute a set of $N$ chromatograms of the form $(\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{c},\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{t})$, one for each sequence in the database. These chromatograms are then further processed to get predicted PSSMs. This step is illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:PreprocessingScheme}.B. \end{enumerate} After performing these two steps, and additional alignment step is required to match the start of the measure and predicted chromatograms.
input: a training set $S'$ of known sequences and their chromatograms
nodes.statement_short: Learn 6-mer peak height/position tables from training chromatograms, predict a PSSM for every database sequence, then align with the measurement.

nodes.name: Compute local-sequence statistics
nodes.statement: A preliminary step: Compute local-sequence adjusted chromatogram statistics. \\ Here we use a training set $S'$ of known sequences and their chromatograms as input and compute tables $H$ and $P$ representing chromatogram peak heights and positions, respectively, for different local-sequence contexts.
nodes.statement_short: Estimate the peak height and position tables $H,P$ from a training set.

nodes.name: Generate predicted PSSMs
nodes.statement: Database PSSMs Generation step: Generate a database of predicted PSSMs. \\ Here the input is a set $S$ of $N$ sequences and the pre-computed tables $H$ and $P$. The sequence input and tables are used to determine peak heights and positions and compute a set of $N$ chromatograms of the form $(\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{c},\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{t})$, one for each sequence in the database. These chromatograms are then further processed to get predicted PSSMs. This step is illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:PreprocessingScheme}.B.
nodes.statement_short: Predict a chromatogram, then a PSSM, for each database sequence.

nodes.name: Align measured and predicted chromatograms
nodes.statement: After performing these two steps, and additional alignment step is required to match the start of the measure and predicted chromatograms.
nodes.statement_short: Align the start of measured and predicted chromatograms.

nodes.name: Training peak positions $p_{i,j}$ and heights $h_{i,j}$
nodes.statement: We use $p_{i,j}$ and $h_{i,j}$ to denote the position and height of the $j$-th nucleotide in the $i$-th sequence, respectively (we have chosen the top peak out of the four traces representing different bases - since each chromatogram represented a single sequence, these peaks were in most cases clearly higher and distinguishable from the three other peaks).
nodes.section: B.1 Preliminary Step: Compute local-sequence adjusted chromatogram statistics

nodes.name: Local sequence context is the preceding 5 nucleotides (6-mer)
nodes.statement: We have modeled the local sequence context by looking at the $5$ nucleotides preceding each nucleotide, giving us $4^6 = 4096$ different unique 6-mers, each representing a possible nucleotide and the $5$ nucleotides preceding it.
nodes.section: B.1 Preliminary Step: Compute local-sequence adjusted chromatogram statistics
nodes.statement_short: Peak height and position depend on the nucleotide and its 5 predecessors, a 6-mer among $4^6=4096$.

nodes.name: Peak height statistic $H(\alpha)$
nodes.statement: More formally, for a given kmer $\alpha = (\alpha_1,..,\alpha_6)$, we have computed $H(\alpha)$ and $P(\alpha)$ as follows. The peak height statistic $H(\alpha)$ measures the corresponding local-averaged peak heights: \begin{equation} H(\alpha) = \frac{\sum_{i,j} 1_{\{\alpha_1 = S'_{i,j-5}, ..,\alpha_6 = S'_{i,j}\}} h_{i,j}} {\sum_{i,j} 1_{\{\alpha_1 = S'_{i,j-5}, ..,\alpha_6 = S'_{i,j}\}}} \end{equation}
nodes.section: B.1 Preliminary Step: Compute local-sequence adjusted chromatogram statistics
nodes.statement_short: $H(\alpha)$ is the average training peak height at positions whose 6-mer context is $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Peak height statistic (B.1)
nodes.section: B.1 Preliminary Step: Compute local-sequence adjusted chromatogram statistics
nodes.label: eq:peak_height

nodes.name: Relative peak-peak distance $d_{i,j}$
nodes.statement: \noindent For peak position $P(\alpha)$, we first computed the relative peak-peak distance for each position: \begin{equation} d_{i,j} = \frac{p_{i,j}-p_{i,j-1}}{\sum_{j=2}^k p_{i,j}-p_{i,j-1}}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: B.1 Preliminary Step: Compute local-sequence adjusted chromatogram statistics

nodes.name: Relative peak-peak distance (B.2)
nodes.section: B.1 Preliminary Step: Compute local-sequence adjusted chromatogram statistics

nodes.name: Peak position statistic $P(\alpha)$
nodes.statement: \noindent Then, we measured the average relative peak-peak distance between the current peak and the previous peak: \begin{equation} P(\alpha) = \frac{\sum_{i,j} 1_{\{\alpha_1 = S'_{i,j-5}, ..,\alpha_6 = S'_{i,j}\}} d_{i,j}} {\sum_{i,j} 1_{\{\alpha_1 = S'_{i,j-5}, ..,\alpha_6 = S'_{i,j}\}}} \end{equation}
nodes.section: B.1 Preliminary Step: Compute local-sequence adjusted chromatogram statistics
nodes.statement_short: $P(\alpha)$ is the average relative peak-peak distance at positions with 6-mer context $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Peak position statistic (B.3)
nodes.section: B.1 Preliminary Step: Compute local-sequence adjusted chromatogram statistics
nodes.label: eq:peak_position

nodes.name: Context-dependent variability of peak height and position
nodes.statement: While the average height and position were $1$ (as was ensured by our normalizations), there was significant variability in height and position according to sequence context, with height values $H$ typically in the range $\sim\! 0.5\!-\!1.3$ and position values $P$ in the range $\sim\! 0.8\!-\!1.2$ (see Figure \ref{fig:PosHeightDist}).
nodes.section: B.1 Preliminary Step: Compute local-sequence adjusted chromatogram statistics
nodes.statement_short: Across 6-mers, height ranges about 0.5-1.3 and position 0.8-1.2 around a mean of 1.

nodes.name: Position drift parameter $\beta$
nodes.statement: An additional sequence-independent non-linearity in the peak position was observed in the chromatograms studied, where distance between consecutive peak increases as we move further along the chromatogram. This was accounted for by fitting an additional linear model based only on the nucleotide sequence position, giving an additional parameter of $\beta = 0.00036$ representing increase in peak-peak distance with each position (see next section in eq. (\ref{eq:peak_params_estimation}) ).
nodes.section: B.1 Preliminary Step: Compute local-sequence adjusted chromatogram statistics
nodes.statement_short: A linear fit in position adds $\beta=0.00036$ to the peak-peak distance per position.

nodes.name: Database PSSM generation (predicted chromatograms)
nodes.statement: The input for this step is the database sequence matrix $S$ and the output is a set of PSSMs $(a, c, g, t)^t$, one for each sequence $S_i$ in the database. The database processing scheme is applied only once to the database and the predicted PSSMs are stored and can be used for any new mixture sample obtained. It is applied to each sequence in the database independently. For every nucleotide in the database, we estimated it's chromatogram peak height and peak-peak distance as: \begin{equation} a_{i,j}=H( L_{i,j} ), \quad b_{i,j}=b_{i,j-1}+P (L_{i,j} )+ \beta j \end{equation} where $L_{i,j} = (S_{i,j-5},..,S_{i,j})$ denotes the local 6-mer sequence context of nucleotide $j$ in the $i$-th sequence ($L_{i,j} \in 1 ... 4^6 $). The parameter $\beta = 0.00036$ represents the increase in peak-peak distance per position as we move further along the sequence. In order to generate a chromatogram trace for a given sequence, each peak was modeled as a Gaussian centered at the peak position and with height equal to the peak height. Thus, for every nucleotide in a sequence, a corresponding peak was created in the chromatogram using the Gaussian peak function \begin{equation} f_{i,j}(x)=a_{i,j} e^{- \frac{(x-b_{i,j})^2}{2c^2}} \end{equation} The widths of the chromatogram Gaussian peaks were approximated by using a constant peak width obtained by setting $c=0.4$. A chromatogram was generated for each sequence by summing the values of obtained $f_{i,j}$ over all nucleotides. Each $f_{i,j}$ was evaluated for $x$ values equally spaced in the range $[0,k]$, at a resolution of $1/12$ thus giving $12 k$ different $x$ values $x_1,..,x_{12 k}$. Each $f_{i,j}$ contributed to the sum only for the trace of the corresponding base in the sequence, and for the other three bases the contribution to the sum was zero. That is, the trace vector for the nucleotide 'A' for the $i$-th sequence was computed as: \begin{equation} \mathfrak{a}_{p} = \sum_j f_{i, j } (x_p) 1_{\{S_{i,j} = 'A'\}} \end{equation} and similarly for the other three nucleotides. The resulting predicted chromatograms were binned using a constant bin size of $1$ and transformed via square root, in similar to the chromatogram preprocessing step in eq. (\ref{eq:sqrt_binning}), to give a PSSM database with one PSSM for each sequence in $S$.
nodes.section: B.2 Database PSSMs Generation step: Generate a database of predicted PSSMs.
output: a set of PSSMs $(a, c, g, t)^t$, one for each sequence $S_i$ in the database
nodes.statement_short: For each database sequence, predict peak heights and positions from 6-mer tables, sum Gaussian peaks into traces, then bin and square-root into a PSSM.

nodes.name: Alignment of predicted and measured chromatograms
nodes.statement: We are therefore faced with the problem of correctly aligning the initial bin position in the measured chromatogram and the bin positions of the predicted chromatograms.
nodes.section: B.3 Alignment of Predicted and Measured Chromatograms

nodes.name: Offset selection by minimal reconstruction distance
nodes.statement: This was solved by trying the {\textbf {BCS} } reconstruction for different initial bin offsets in the measured chromatogram, and selecting for the offset with the lowest reconstruction root square distance (see Figure \ref{fig:ChromatogramOffset}.A). This reconstruction root square distance is calculated as the difference between the measured chromatogram and the predicted chromatogram based the reconstructed species frequencies.
nodes.section: B.3 Alignment of Predicted and Measured Chromatograms
nodes.statement_short: Run BCS for each initial bin offset and keep the offset whose reconstruction best matches the measured chromatogram.

nodes.name: Try offsets and select the best
nodes.statement: This was solved by trying the {\textbf {BCS} } reconstruction for different initial bin offsets in the measured chromatogram, and selecting for the offset with the lowest reconstruction root square distance (see Figure \ref{fig:ChromatogramOffset}.A).
nodes.section: B.3 Alignment of Predicted and Measured Chromatograms
nodes.statement_short: Run BCS per offset; pick the lowest root square distance.

nodes.name: Compute reconstruction distance
nodes.statement: This reconstruction root square distance is calculated as the difference between the measured chromatogram and the predicted chromatogram based the reconstructed species frequencies.
nodes.section: B.3 Alignment of Predicted and Measured Chromatograms
nodes.statement_short: Distance between measured and reconstruction-predicted chromatograms.

nodes.name: Offset criterion validated with the known composition
nodes.statement: To verify the validity of this criterion, we also compared the average distance between the measured chromatogram and the predicted mixture chromatogram obtained using the known mixture composition (see Figure \ref{fig:ChromatogramOffset}.B), using various offsets for the measured chromatogram binning. Both methods obtained an identical offset, which was used in the reconstruction.
nodes.section: B.3 Alignment of Predicted and Measured Chromatograms
nodes.statement_short: Using the known composition gives the same offset as the reconstruction-based criterion.
